translations.text: Discourse of our holy father Basil to the rich.
We have already spoken before, at another time, about this young man of whom we have now read in the Gospel, I know,
for the diligent hearer remembers everything that we said then, first of all that this is not the same man as the lawyer of whom Luke speaks.
For that man was a tester and questioned with scorn, whereas this one questioned well, but did not receive the answer obediently.
For if his question had been asked with contempt, he would not have gone away grieved at the words of the Lord.
For this reason the holy Gospel shows his mind as something mixed: on one side praiseworthy, and on the other side wretched and utterly lost.

For that he recognized the true teacher, and passed over the arrogance of the Pharisees, the pride of the lawyers and the vanity [?] of the scribes, and gave the name of teacher to the true teacher, this was praiseworthy.
And that he also took care how the inheritance of eternal life comes about, this too was acceptable.
But the Gospel exposes his mind and his will, showing that he was not looking toward the true good, but toward what appears pleasing in the eyes of the many.
For he learned the teaching of life from the true teacher, and did not write it on his heart, nor did he carry out in deed what he had been taught, but went away grieved,
darkened by the passion of love of riches; and this exposes the unsettledness of his mind and his failure to bear witness to himself.
Tell me, you call him teacher, and yet you do not do what disciples do?
You confess him to be good, and yet you turn away what he gives? For one who is good is without doubt also a giver of goodness.
And you ask about eternal life, yet you are wholly nailed to this passing life?
Or what hard, heavy and immoderate word did the teacher say to you? Did he not say this: "Sell your possessions and give to the poor"?
For if he had commanded you the toil of labor, or the storms of trading at sea,
or any other of the hardships that belong to those who seek a livelihood, then you would have had reason to be grieved at that command.
But if by so easy a road, which has neither toil nor hardship, he has promised to lead you to eternal life, do you not rejoice at the ease of that salvation?
Instead you go away sorrowful and grieving in soul, and you make all your earlier labor useless.
For if you have not killed anyone, as you say, nor committed adultery, nor stolen, nor borne false witness against anyone,
you make all this diligence profitless for yourself, for you do not add even that which is lacking, by which alone you could enter the kingdom of heaven.
And if some physician were telling you to make good some deficiency of your limbs, which had come upon you by nature or through disease, you would not be grieved at it.
Since, then, the great physician of souls is eager to make you whole, you who lack those better members, do you not accept that grace, but instead mourn and grieve?
It is evident, then, that you are far from that commandment, and that you falsely claimed it for yourself when you said that you have loved your neighbor as yourself.
For behold, this word of the Lord convicts you, showing that you are far from true love.
For if that word of yours were true, and you had kept the commandment of love from your youth, and had given to each person as much
as to yourself, where would this wealth of possessions have come to you from?
For giving to the poor is what uses up wealth, when each person is given what he needs, and it is evident that:
whoever loves his neighbor as himself has nothing more than his neighbor has.
But behold, it is plain that you have great property. Where has it all come from?
Only from this: that you have reckoned your own comfort more precious than the comfort of others. And the more you exceed others in wealth,
by so much you lack love; for otherwise, if you had loved your neighbor, you would long ago have been anxious to disperse that property.
But now possessions mean more to you than even the limbs of your body, and being parted from them distresses you like the cutting off of limbs.
For if you had clothed the naked, if you had given your bread to the hungry, if your door had been open to every stranger,
if you had become a father to orphans and had pitied everyone who is weak, what possessions would you now be grieving over?
Or how would the loss of what remained have seemed hard to you [?], if from the first you had been anxious to distribute all of it among the poor?
Or do you not see how in the marketplace no one is grieved when he gives what he has and receives what he does not have?
Rather, the smaller the price at which he buys something worth more, the more he rejoices, as over having traded splendidly and well.
But are you grieved because you give gold and silver and possessions, which are stone and earth, in order to gain that blessed life?
And for what would you use that wealth of yours? To clothe yourself in splendid garments?
A garment of two cubits is enough for you, and wearing one garment will serve the purpose of those many-colored garments.
Or would you use wealth for food? But one loaf is enough to fill the belly.
Why then are you grieved? What are you being deprived of? Of the glory that is given to you by wealth?
But if you do not seek glory on earth, you will find that true and splendid glory which will be given to you in the kingdom of heaven.
Or do you say that wealth is lovable in itself, even if there is no profit from it?
But this is evident to everyone, that the immeasurable acquisition of possessions and money is unprofitable.
Yet let me tell you something else as well, and though it may seem astonishing to you, it is true, namely that:
if you disperse wealth in the way the Lord commanded, it will all the more remain with you, and if you are greedy, then it will be scattered.
If you hold on to it, you do not have it; but if you scatter it, it will not be lost to you, for it is written:
"He has scattered abroad and given to the poor, and his righteousness endures forever."
But it is not for the sake of clothing and food that wealth is so beloved by some; rather, the devil has found some device and suggests to the rich countless pretexts for spending,
so that they gather what is superfluous and useless with as much zeal as if it were something necessary for their use.
And nothing at all is ever enough for their means of spending, for they divide that wealth into expenses for the time in which they are living and again for times to come;
and some of the money they keep for themselves, and again some for their children.
Then again they divide it for spending on this and that affair. For see what their arrangements are, namely:
"Let this money be for use, and let this other be stored away in treasuries," and what is for use is not only for necessities, but for useless things:
"And again let this money be for adorning the house, and again this for those outward displays and ornaments, and this for when we go on a journey, and again that for when we are at home,
so that our life may be splendid, with pleasure and luxury." But I am astonished at those useless excesses of theirs,
how they have countless carriages, some for themselves and some for other use, covered with gold and silver,
and horses likewise beyond number, which are given names just like men, each being named after the lineage of its fathers and grandfathers:
some for riding in the city when they take their pleasure, others again for going out to the hunt, others again made ready for journeys and battles,
on which are saddles and bridles and coverings, all gilded, all sewn with silver thread, and halters of purple.
And they adorn those horses like brides. Then again a multitude of mules, sorted by color;
their grooms, following one after another, others again running ahead, others going alongside;
a countless multitude of other servants, troops of slaves, eager for every kind of luxury.
Again, over them other stewards and overseers, some personal attendants, some laborers;
others again practitioners of every craft, some of useful work and some of vain work devised for pleasure;
cooks, bakers, wine-cellar keepers, hunters, painters, the doers and fulfillers of every desire.
Multitudes of camels, some carrying loads and some grazing;
herds of horses, droves of cattle, flocks of sheep, herds of swine, and herdsmen for all of these.
All the land acquired for pleasure, increasing that wealth by its revenue.
Baths in the city, baths in the villages, halls adorned with marbles of various kinds:
one with Phrygian stone, another again with Laconian or Thessalonian, or Roman.
And these were of such kinds that some warmed in winter and others cooled in summer.
The floor is adorned with a mosaic of tiny stones, the ceiling is plastered with gold, and the walls are adorned with upright slabs of marble;
and whatever lies above the marble they paint with all kinds of figures.
And then, when that wealth has been divided up ten thousand ways and there is still more left over, they commit it to the ground, bury it, and store it away in hidden places, saying:
"Who knows what will happen in the times to come? Perhaps unexpected events may occur."
Man, who knows whether you will ever use it at all? For that is uncertain, but this mercilessness and wickedness of yours is not uncertain.
For when you could not use up your wealth by all those many devices of yours, you then hid it in the ground. Alas, what evil madness!
As long as the gold was in the "eyes" [?] of the earth, you dug and searched for it, and when it came to light and emerged from there, you bury it there again and make it vanish.
And then, as I suppose, when you have buried your wealth, you bury your heart along with it, for it says: "Where your treasures are, there your hearts will be also."
This is why the commandments distress the rich: they consider it death if they are not amusing themselves with those useless expenditures.
And I think that this affliction of this young man and of those like him resembles the case of a man
who, out of desire for a certain city, travels a long road in order to see it, and when he comes close to its walls,
through neglect of a little further walking he renders all his great labor useless and does not become worthy of seeing the good things of that city.
Such are those who do much else but are unwilling to part with their money.
For I have seen many who fasted, prayed, sighed, and displayed that struggle which costs nothing, yet would not bring themselves to give a single small coin to those in distress.
What will their other striving profit them, since the kingdom of heaven cannot hold them? For the Lord himself said:
"It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven."
This verdict is plain to see: the one who spoke it does not lie, but those who obey it are few. Yet they say:
"And how are we to live once we have scattered everything? Or what would this world look like if everyone divided up their possessions?"
Do not ask me for the reason behind the commands of the King. The Lawgiver knows how to make his own law possible to keep.
But your heart is being tested, as if on a scale, as to whether your intention inclines toward the true life or toward this passing ease.
For one must know that wealth has been given not for one's own enjoyment, but to be managed for the benefit of others.

And when it is being given to the poor, joy is what is fitting, as if we were being set free from things stored up that belong to others, and not grief, as if we were being made strangers to what is our own.
Why then are you sad, and why do you mourn over the word that says, "Sell your possessions"?

For even if your possessions were to follow you into that age to come, even then they should not be loved, because beside the honor of the good things there, these good things of this world would become invisible.
If, then, beyond any doubt all these things must be left behind here, why do we not sell them and take their profit away with us?
But you, when you hand over gold and get a horse, are not grieved. Yet when you hand over these perishable things and the kingdom of heaven is given to you, do you weep over it?
You refuse the one who asks you. You do not want to give, and you gather countless excuses.
What will you answer the Judge? You who decorate walls, will you not clothe a human being?
You who cover horses with gold, do you ignore your brother who is shamefully naked? You who let wheat rot, will you not feed the hungry?
You who bury gold, if you see a debtor being choked by his creditor, will you treat him with contempt?
And if his wife is also found to be of the same mind, the disease is doubled. She multiplies luxuries, increases the love of fine tastes, and becomes a goad to desire.
They acquire stones of some kind, pearls, emeralds, jacinths and gold. Some of it they have hammered and some woven, and in every way they make that disease grow,
for they do not pursue these matters in passing. Night and day they are anxious about them.
And they gather craftsmen of every kind: they bring in dyers of brilliant dyes, goldsmiths, perfumers, weavers of gold, and painters.
They never have any rest, and no amount of wealth is enough to fulfil their desires, not even if it flowed up from a river,
when that foreign perfume is sought after as if it were ordinary oil from the market streets, and again those beautiful things that come out of the sea:
the murex shell and the pinna, more than sheep's wool. And gold is set around those costly stones:
some becomes a band for the forehead, some a necklace, other gold is spent on belts, other gold on the rings they put on their hands, and the rest on ornaments for the feet.
For these gold-lovers are glad to have their hands and feet bound, as long as gold is what binds them.
But when would such a man ever care for his own soul, when he is serving these evil desires of defilement?
For as a ship is wrecked by the violence of the waves and lost, so the desires of women sink those pitiable souls.
And when the wealth of these lovers of desire is spent like this on such things,
Such a man never reaches out to the poor; instead he lets himself be lured into acquiring vain things. And if he hears:
"Sell your possessions and give to the poor, so that you may have provision for the journey to eternal life," he goes away grieved. But if he hears:

"Give money to the women singers," or "Give it to the stonecutters, the goldsmiths, the builders, the gold-inlay workers [?], the painters," he rejoices, as though he were receiving something precious and worth more than the money.
O man, do you not see these walls, ruined by the passing of time? Only parts of them are left in the city, and they lie there only to trip up people walking by.
How many poor people must there have been in this city when these walls were being put up? The rich ignored them because they were so eager to build.
So where now is their brilliant decoration? Or where is the man who was envied for building them?
Are these not destroyed and laid waste, like those buildings that children make of sand at play?
And the man who made them now lies in hell and repents of his vain striving.
May you have a great and splendid soul; for do not walls, small and great alike, serve one and the same purpose?
For when I enter the house of a proud and insatiably rich man and see that house adorned with every beauty, I begin to mourn,
for I understand that this man holds nothing more precious than these visible things; he adorns those soulless things, while his soul is ugly.
Or tell me, what greater service do silver beds and silver tables perform,
ivory chairs and splendid seats, that because of them your wealth cannot be given to the poor?
Yet multitudes stand at your doors, speaking every pitiful word to you, but you refuse to give and say:
"My possessions will not suffice to give to all those poor people."
With your tongue you swear that you have nothing, but your hand convicts you, for your hand silently proclaims your lie, since it shines with the gem of the ring that is on it.
How many distressed debtors could one ring from your finger set free? How many collapsing houses could it set upright?
One chest of yours, full of your clothes, could clothe a great many people afflicted by the cold.
But you can bear to send that poor man away empty-handed, and you do not fear the just retribution from the Judge.
Have you shown no mercy? Neither will you find mercy. Have you not opened your door to the poor man?
You too will be driven out of the kingdom. Have you not given bread? Neither will eternal life be given to you.
Or do you call yourself poor? I too bear you witness in this, for the poor man is he who needs many things and does not have them.
And that insatiability of desires makes you the same, for on top of ten talents you hasten to acquire another ten, and when they have become twenty, you seek as many more.
And what keeps coming in does not satisfy your will, but always kindles you to desire still more.
For just as drinking itself becomes the cause of further drinking for drunkards, so too the rich, when they have gained much, long for still more,
and the more they gain, the more that disease grows, and that striving turns all the more to the opposite of what they seek.
For what they have gained does not gladden them, but what they have not gained distresses them, and their soul constantly melts away with care as they strive after excess.
For they ought to rejoice and give thanks to God that they are richer than so many, but instead they mourn because they fall short in wealth of some one or two.
When they have caught up with one rich man in wealth, they then hasten to reach a richer one, and if they catch up with him too, they then turn their striving toward another.
Just as those climbing a ladder always lift their foot to the higher rung and do not stop until they reach the top of the ladder,
so too these men do not cease from striving until they have risen very high and, falling from that great height, are shattered.
The bird called the seleucid was created insatiable by the Creator of all for the good of humankind, but you have made your soul insatiable to the harm of many.
As much as the eye sees, so much does greed desire: "the eye is not filled with seeing," nor is the lover of silver sated with gain.
Hell has not said, "It is enough," nor does greed ever say, "It is enough." When will you use all of that?
When will you find rest from those things, since you are always held fast by the affliction of acquiring?
Woe to those who join house to house and bring field next to field, so as to seize something belonging to their neighbor.
And you, what do you do? Do you not find countless pretexts for seizing your neighbor's property? You talk like this:
"My neighbor's house blocks my light; it causes me trouble," or "It does me some other harm." Pretexts never run out.
And so you would harass him and afflict him until you had driven him away from what was his own. What killed Naboth the Israelite?
Was it not Ahab's desire for that vineyard? Greed is an evil neighbor to live with in the city, and evil in the countryside.
The sea knows its boundary, and the night does not transgress its appointed order, but greed has no regard for the time and knows no limit;
it does not spare what has been an inheritance from of old, but is like the violence of fire: it advances upon everything and devours everything.
And just as a river first finds a small outlet and begins to flow along that track, and then grows little by little, and whatever is found before it,
it sweeps all of it away, so too the rich receive from those they have oppressed the power for still greater oppression, and the more people they oppress,
the greater the power that comes to them, and the very magnitude of their wickedness becomes what adds to their strength.
For those who have been wickedly oppressed by them give them forced assistance in oppressing and subjugating others as well.
For what neighbor, what fellow resident, what seller is not oppressed? Nothing withstands that affliction of wealth:
everything yields to its tyranny, everything fears it, and each of the oppressed looks only to whether he will bring yet some other evil upon him,
not to hastening to court over what was seized. For he carries off the yokes of oxen, seizes another's land,
plows, sows, and reaps what is not his own. If the poor man resists, blows are immediately ready; if he laments, he reviles him;
if he goes to court, he is shut up in prison, for false witnesses are ready, who bring the oppressed man to the fear of death.
He wishes he could give up something else besides, if only he might escape from him.
I wish, O rich and rapacious man, that for just a short time you would grant yourself relief from those labors of injustice and give your mind some leisure,
so that you might understand and consider toward what end this eagerness of yours is hastening so.
See, you have this great abundance of land, of fields and vineyards, mountains and plains, rivers and meadows.
What then is to come after all of that? Will not three cubits of earth be given you out of all of that?
Will not the weight of a few stones be enough to cover that wretched body of yours?
Why do you hurry? Why do you act lawlessly? Why do you gather fruitlessness with your own hand?
And would that it were only fruitlessness, and not fuel for the eternal fire! Will you not at last sober up from that drunkenness of yours?
Will you not restore your mind to health? Will you not come back to yourself? Will you not set before your eyes the judgment seat of Christ?
What will you answer when those you have oppressed and afflicted surround you and cry out against you before the righteous Judge?
What will you do? What helpers in speech and advocates will you hire? What witnesses will you bring forward? How will you deceive that Judge who knows all?
There is no philosopher [?] there, no duplicity of words and their truth made of lies, which could steal away the Judge's truth.
Those flatterers will not be with you then; no bribe will be with you there, nor the glory of your rank.
You will be bereft of friends, bereft of helpers, without an advocate, without a word to say, put to shame. They will lead you away sorrowful, with bowed head, left alone, terrified.
For wherever you turn your eye, you will plainly see the images of your evil deeds:
on this side the tears of the orphan, on that side the sighs of the widow, on another side the poor whom you have beaten;
the servants whom you flogged, the neighbors whom you oppressed: all will rise up against you. The wicked camp of your wicked deeds will surround you.
For as a shadow follows the body, so its sins follow the soul, clearly depicting its deeds.
Therefore there is no denial there, but every shameless mouth is stopped.
For there each person's own deeds bear witness against him, not by uttering a voice, but by appearing just as they were done by us.
How can I set those terrors before you? Perhaps you may listen; perhaps you may turn back.
Remember that day when "wrath is revealed from heaven"; remember the glorious coming of Christ,
when "those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
Then eternal shame will be spread over sinners, and "the fury of fire that devours sinners."
Let that trouble you, and let not the commandment trouble you. How can I soften you? What shall I say?
Do you not long for the kingdom? Do you not fear Gehenna? Where can healing be found for your soul?
For if terrible things do not frighten you and radiant things do not make you long for them, are we then speaking to a heart of stone?
Consider, O man, the nature of wealth. Why are you so stupefied by the love of gold?
Gold is a stone, and silver too is a stone; the pearl is a stone, and every precious gem is a stone.
Chrysolite and beryl and jacinth and amethyst and jasper: these are the precious things of wealth,
Some of these you bury, hiding those brilliant stones in darkness, and others you wear on your fingers, and you pride yourself on them because of their color.
Tell me, what benefit do you get from those stones? Are you not ashamed of the glitter of your hand? For you crave stones, as women do when they are bearing children.
For they chew on stones, and you waste away for the sake of stones, and you seek out sardonyx and jasper and amethyst.
Who has been able by adornment to add a single day to his life? Whom has death avoided because of wealth?
From whom has sickness departed because of money? How long will gold remain the destruction of souls, the forge of death, the snare of sin?
How long will wealth remain the cause of wars, for whose sake weapons are forged and for whose sake swords are sharpened?
Because of it, kinsmen become ignorant of their own nature, and brothers look on one another with murderous intent.
Because of wealth there are robbers in the deserts, plotters on the seas, and slanderers in the cities.
Who is the father of lies? Who is the producer of unlawful writing? Who is the parent of false swearing? Is it not wealth?
Is it not the eager pursuit of it? What has come over you, O man? Who has turned that helper of yours into your enemy?
For goods have been given as a help to life, not as a cause of evils; as a ransom for the soul, not as a guide to destruction.
But you say that wealth is good for the sake of your children.
This is the first pretext of avarice: you put forward your children as a pretext, yet you cannot satisfy your own hearts. Do not bring forward as a pretext the one who is not to blame.
He has his own King, his own Governor; he has his life not from you but from God, and from him too he awaits deliverance [?].
Was the Gospel perhaps not written for married people as well, which says: "If you wish to be perfect, sell your possessions and give to the poor"?
When you asked the Lord for the gift of children, when you implored him that you might become a father of children, did you perhaps also say this:
Give me children so that I may disobey your commandments? Give me children so that I may not reach the kingdom of heaven?
Or who will be guarantor for that child, that he will make good use of what is given to him? For wealth has become a cause of defilement for many.
Have you not heard what Solomon says: "I have seen a grievous sickness: wealth kept by its owner to his own harm"?
And again he says: "I leave it to the man who comes after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or foolish?"
Take care lest with much toil you gather that wealth, and supply [?] others with an occasion of sin, and then be found punished twice over:
for the sins you committed yourself and for those of which you became the cause for others. Or is it not your own soul, above all, that is closest to you in kinship?
First give it a share of the inheritance, give it the rich means of life, and then divide your possessions among your children.
For children often receive nothing from their parents and acquire property for themselves, but your soul, if you abandon it, who will have mercy on it?
These words are addressed to those who have children; but as for the childless, what manifold pretext for their avarice do they put before us?
For thus the greedy man says: "I will not sell my possessions; I will not give to the needy poor what serves the needs of this life."
So then, the Lord is not your teacher, nor is the holy Gospel the law of your life; rather, you yourself are the lawgiver for yourself.
But see into what evil you fall through such thoughts.
For if the Lord has commanded us this and you say it cannot be done, you are doing nothing other than showing yourself wiser than the Lord. Or else you say this:
"Let me enjoy myself during these days of my life, and after I die I will make the poor the heirs of my possessions; by a written deed and a will I will make them masters of my wealth"?
What then is this thing you are saying? When you are no longer counted among men, will you then become a lover of mankind?
When I see you dead, shall I then call you a lover of your brothers?
Great indeed is the grace of that mercy of yours, for lying in the grave and turned to earth you have become so generous and so kind in giving away your possessions!
Or for which times are you seeking grace and reward? Tell me: for the times of your life, or for those you spent after death?

For during the days when you were alive, you were corrupted in pleasures and delights and lusts and did not even wish to look at the poor; and when you have died, what deed of yours is there any longer?
Or what will your reward be? Show your deeds, and then seek your reward.
After the market has been taken down, no one trades any more; after the contest has broken up, no one who arrives is crowned;
after the fighters have gone, no one fights, and neither does anyone practice virtue after death.
Do you promise me with ink and paper that you will do mercy? Who then has told you the time of your end?
Who is the guarantor and informant of the manner in which you are to depart from here?
How many have been snatched away in an instant by grievous events, without even being able to speak a word? How many has fever of the head [?] rendered senseless?
Why then do you wait for that time in which perhaps you will not even be master of your mind? Dark night will come, and heavy sickness, and no helper will appear anywhere;
and the one who is to receive your possessions will be at the ready, arranging everything according to his own will, and your plans will become useless.
Then you will look around here and there and see the desolation surrounding you; then you will understand how badly you planned;
then you will groan over your foolishness, that you were keeping the commandment for such a time,
when your tongue will be mute and your hand trembling, and you can neither say anything in words nor write with your hand and make known your thought.
For even if everything had been clearly written down and well proclaimed, one altered letter would be able to overturn all of it,
or one altered seal, or else two or three witnesses, would assign all those possessions to others.
Why then do you deceive yourself, and now manage that wealth badly on the lusts of the flesh, and make your pledge at the very last, when you will no longer be master of those affairs?
It is as if we were to say, oh evil plan: "As long as I am alive, let me enjoy myself with lusts, and when I die, then I will fulfill the commandments."
To you too Abraham will say: "You received your good things in your life."
That narrow and difficult way will not admit you while you are clothed in the bulk of your wealth, with which you departed, not having stripped it off as the Lord commanded you.
While you were alive, you took no thought for life; when you were dying, you honored the commandment more than your enemies, you who wrote thus:
"So that so-and-so may not receive it, let the Lord receive it." But what name shall we give to this deed?
Vengeance on enemies, or love of neighbor? Read your will again: did you not write thus at the beginning:
"I wished for life and for joy in my possessions, but since I am departing, now let it be as you say"?
The credit belongs to death, not to you, for if you had not been dying, you would not have remembered that commandment.
"Do not be deceived; God is not mocked." A dead thing does not enter the altar; offer a living sacrifice.
For whoever offers from what is surplus, his offering is unacceptable; and you, will you offer to the Good One that which was left over after your whole life?
Or would you dare to entertain the king's nobles with the leftovers of your table?
How then do you dare to give God an offering from the leftovers of your whole life?
See the end to which love of money comes, O rich, and cease from being so passionately in love with gold.
The more you love glory, the more you should leave nothing of your possessions behind. Make everything your own, take everything with you.
Do not leave your wealth to strangers, who perhaps will not even tend to you properly, but will bury you just as you were found.
And your servants will turn to the heirs, who perhaps will even philosophize over you and say:
"Adorning a dead man and carrying out with honor one who knows nothing is foolishness.
Is it not better that those who are here be adorned with that clothing, rather than that it rot with the dead man?
Or what use to a dead man are a finely polished tomb and useless expense?
It is better to use these goods in this life than to waste them on him."
So your attendants and servants will speak, taking revenge on you and currying favor with your successors.
Anticipate them, then, and bury yourself well. A good burial is godliness.
Clothe yourself with all that is yours and so depart. Make your wealth a true adornment for yourself.
Have it with you. Listen to Christ, that good counselor, who loved you, who became poor for our sake,
so that we might become rich through his poverty, who gave himself as a ransom for us.
Either let us listen to him as a wise and better counselor, or as one who loves us, and let us believe and do his word, what he commanded us,
so that we may inherit eternal life through the same Christ, to whom belong glory and might, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
